cells.tense: Now you're carrying what you said you'd carry, and the people around you are naming it out loud.
cells.act: tend the resource with responsible care
cells.ask: Choose a load you carry for other people and tend it deliberately — check it, straighten it, keep it in good order — without saying you did.
cells.core:
You're bearing something on behalf of other people, and it's being seen for what it is. The effort and the recognition roughly match. That match is what keeps endurance from turning into either a grind or a performance, and when it's present, you can hold a lot without it hollowing you out.

The work now is steady tending. Take one load you carry and keep it in good order on purpose — not more load, the same load, looked after. Tend it like something that depends on your care and will come along if you keep showing up without making a show of it. What you get back is the plain fact of the thing being in good shape because you kept it that way.

cells.tense: Tomorrow's version of the load is already in your arms, and today's hasn't even landed yet.
cells.act: strike one thing from the list that does not serve
cells.ask: Cross an item off the list — the one you could set down without catastrophe — and watch what happens when you don't pick it up again.
cells.core:
You're bracing against a weight that isn't here yet. The acknowledgment that would complete the last thing you carried hasn't come, or you've decided it won't, so you take on the next load early and hold it in advance. Endurance run this way stops being strength and becomes a stance you take toward a future you can't write. When it's working, the load you finished is allowed to be finished, and surrender there reads as fulfillment rather than defeat.

Strike that item. Put it down, let the pressure land where it lands, and watch without stepping back in to take it up again. What you get is a true reading of which loads actually need you, taken without the noise of a list written in advance.

cells.tense: You carried it and then stood at a door that had already closed behind you.
cells.act: persist on your own reserves through the pressure
cells.ask: Carry the smallest load you already have on your own effort — nothing but your own reserves, no one checking in, everything else left where it sits.
cells.core:
What you gave up has been given. But the end of it didn't arrive as an end — you're where the weight used to be, holding a shape that has nothing left to hold. Endurance without a completion becomes a pose you keep, and the thing you released doesn't get to be released.

Go small and stay there. Carry one small load, or the smallest part of the one you carry, on your own strength alone. No extra hands, no checking whether it's working, no asking if it's enough. What you get is your own weight in your own arms, which tells you where your strength sits — and where it no longer needs to sit.

cells.tense: You're carrying the load and calling it something else — habit, temperament, no one else's business.
cells.act: look after what grows with a steady hand
cells.ask: Treat a load you carry as something you chose: look after it on purpose, once a day, and know while you do it that the hands are yours.
cells.core:
What you carry here is done by someone you don't count as you. You pick up what no one else picks up and hold it steady, and your account says you just happened to be there. That account is real; you're just not in it. It's what makes the load feel like something that landed on you rather than something you took on.

Steward it as a chosen thing. Take one load and look after it on purpose — a steady hand, one small act of care a day — and know, while you do it, that you are the one doing it. What you get is the same carrying, with you standing where you actually are in it, which is what makes it yours to put down later if you want.
